name: Calcium Gluconate 10% (IV)
indication: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, bradyarrhythmia)
dose: 10 mL of 10% solution (1 g) IV over 2–3 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring; repeat in 5–10 min if ECG changes persist
mechanism: Directly antagonizes cardiac membrane excitability (raises threshold potential) within 1–3 min without lowering serum K+
safetyAlert: Does NOT lower serum K+; follow immediately with Insulin + Dextrose and K+ elimination therapy [Harrison's 22e Ch. 56].

name: Regular Insulin + Dextrose 50% (IV)
indication: Rapid intracellular potassium shift in severe hyperkalemia
dose: 5–10 units IV Regular Insulin + 25–50 g IV Dextrose (omit dextrose if blood glucose >250 mg/dL)
mechanism: Activates Na+/K+-ATPase pump, lowering serum K+ by 0.5–1.2 mEq/L within 15–30 minutes
safetyAlert: Monitor capillary glucose hourly for 4–6 hours; high risk of delayed hypoglycemia in CKD/ESRD patients [Ch. 56].

name: Hypertonic Saline 3% NaCl (IV)
indication: Severely symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, obtundation, coma, herniation risk)
dose: 100 mL IV bolus over 10 minutes (may repeat x2 if severe CNS symptoms persist) to raise Na+ rapidly by 4–6 mEq/L
mechanism: Rapidly reverses cerebral edema by creating osmotic gradient out of brain parenchyma
safetyAlert: NEVER exceed 8–10 mEq/L correction in 24h (4–6 mEq/L max in chronic malnutrition/alcoholism/cirrhosis) to prevent Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome [Ch. 56].

name: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) IV
indication: Any patient with coma, delirium, alcoholism, or malnutrition receiving IV dextrose
dose: 100 mg IV (or 500 mg IV TID if Wernicke encephalopathy suspected) BEFORE or concurrently with 50% Dextrose
mechanism: Essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase; prevents acute precipitation of Wernicke encephalopathy
safetyAlert: Never delay life-saving glucose in confirmed hypoglycemia, but give Thiamine simultaneously/before glucose whenever feasible [Ch. 30].

name: Naloxone (IV / IM / Intranasal)
indication: Suspected opioid overdose (miosis, respiratory depression RR <12, coma)
dose: 0.04–0.4 mg IV titrated every 2–3 min to restore adequate spontaneous ventilation (up to 2–4 mg for synthetic opioids)
safetyAlert: Shorter half-life (30–90 min) than methadone or long-acting opioids — monitor closely for recurrent respiratory depression [Ch. 30].

name: Norepinephrine (IV Infusion)
indication: First-line vasopressor in septic shock and vasodilatory shock unresponsive to crystalloids
dose: Start 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV infusion, titrate to maintain Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) >= 65 mmHg
mechanism: Potent alpha-1 vasoconstrictor with modest beta-1 inotropic support
safetyAlert: Peripheral IV administration is acceptable temporarily while securing central access to avoid delaying MAP restoration [SSC 2021].

name: Ceftriaxone (IV) + Dexamethasone (IV)
indication: Empirical bacterial meningitis / meningococcal fever with petechial rash / Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)
dose: Meningitis: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h (+ Vancomycin + Dexamethasone 10 mg IV before/with 1st antibiotic); SBP: Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV q24h
mechanism: Broad-spectrum 3rd-generation cephalosporin with excellent CSF and ascitic fluid penetration
safetyAlert: NEVER delay first IV antibiotic dose for LP or CT scan in febrile petechial shock or suspected meningitis [Ch. 21, 53].

name: Pantoprazole (IV) + Octreotide (IV)
indication: Acute Upper GI Bleeding (PPI for ulcer bleeding; add Octreotide + Ceftriaxone immediately if cirrhosis/varices suspected)
dose: Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus then 40 mg IV q12h (or 8 mg/h); Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus then 50 mcg/h infusion
mechanism: Elevates gastric pH >6 to stabilize clot; Octreotide reduces splanchnic portal venous pressure
safetyAlert: Pair with restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb <7 g/dL) and upper endoscopy within 24 hours [Ch. 51].
